## Guided Tutorial 11.2: Tracking the Gap Month by Month

**Context and objective.** In Chapter 10 you followed the conversion cost through account 1090 for whole years. In this tutorial, you will measure the gap between the actual cost charged to the account and the standard cost released by completions for each month, accumulate it through each year, compare each month with the same month a year earlier, rank the months, and find what the largest months have in common. You will then rank the work centers by the hours recorded against their planned hours.

**Prerequisites.** Complete Tutorial 11.1, and continue at the end of Chapter11.sql. If you start here, make the working copy as Step 1 of Tutorial 9.1 describes, and download Chapter11.sql as it stands at the end of Tutorial 11.1 from [Companion Files](#sec-companion-files).

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Calculate the monthly gap and its year-to-date total.** The payroll and journal entries debit account 1090 with actual cost, and completions credit it with standard cost. The work order closes, which clear the difference, are left out.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.2: the gap in account 1090 by month and year to date
   SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod,
       ROUND(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit), 2) AS Gap,
       ROUND(SUM(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit)) OVER (
           PARTITION BY FiscalYear ORDER BY FiscalPeriod), 2)
           AS GapYearToDate
   FROM GLEntry
   WHERE AccountID = 92 AND FiscalYear BETWEEN 2024 AND 2026
       AND SourceDocumentType <> 'WorkOrderClose'
   GROUP BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod
   ORDER BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod;
   ```

b. Read the GapYearToDate column in the December row of each year.

The result, shown in @fig-11-05, has one row for each month. The window function sums the monthly gaps within each fiscal year, in order of period, and starts again at zero each January. Each period appears once in its year, so the default window, which includes tied rows, gives a plain running total. The December figure is the year's total gap, and it grew in each year, to nearly twice its fiscal 2024 figure by fiscal 2026. The window works on the results of the grouping, because window functions are calculated after GROUP BY.

![The Monthly Gap in Account 1090 and Its Year-to-Date Total.](/visuals/svg/fig-11-05-gap-year-to-date.svg){#fig-11-05 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor and its result. The editor, on the tab Chapter11.sql, is scrolled to a query that groups the postings to account 1090, without the work order closes, by fiscal year and period, and calculates the monthly gap between actual and standard cost and a year-to-date total with SUM over a window partitioned by fiscal year. The grid shows the twelve months of fiscal 2026, and the GapYearToDate column, which accumulates through the year, is outlined."}

**Step 2. Compare each month with the same month a year earlier.** LAG over a window partitioned by the fiscal period compares each month with the same month of the previous year.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.2: the gap against the same month a year earlier
   SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod,
       ROUND(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit), 2) AS Gap,
       ROUND(LAG(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit)) OVER (
           PARTITION BY FiscalPeriod ORDER BY FiscalYear), 2)
           AS GapSameMonthLastYear
   FROM GLEntry
   WHERE AccountID = 92 AND FiscalYear BETWEEN 2024 AND 2026
       AND SourceDocumentType <> 'WorkOrderClose'
   GROUP BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod
   ORDER BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod;
   ```

b. Compare the Gap and GapSameMonthLastYear columns for the months of fiscal 2026.

GapSameMonthLastYear is NULL for the twelve months of fiscal 2024, which have no earlier year in the data. In most months of fiscal 2026 the gap was larger than in the same month of fiscal 2025. Two comparisons stand out from the rest, though: July 2026 was nearly three times July 2025, and August 2026 was only about half of August 2025. A comparison with the same month removes a seasonal pattern, if there is one, but something else moved the gap in those two months, and the next steps find it.

**Step 3. Rank the months within each year.** A ranking function numbers the months by the size of their gap, and a derived table lets the outer query keep the top three of each year.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.2: the three largest months of each year
   SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod, Gap, GapRank
   FROM (
       SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod,
           ROUND(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit), 2) AS Gap,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY FiscalYear
               ORDER BY SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit) DESC) AS GapRank
       FROM GLEntry
       WHERE AccountID = 92 AND FiscalYear BETWEEN 2024 AND 2026
           AND SourceDocumentType <> 'WorkOrderClose'
       GROUP BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod
   ) AS monthly
   WHERE GapRank <= 3
   ORDER BY FiscalYear, GapRank;
   ```

b. Read the three largest months of each year.

The query returns nine rows, three for each year. The ranking cannot be filtered in the inner query's WHERE clause, because WHERE runs before the window function is calculated. The derived table calculates the rank first, and the outer WHERE keeps the top three. In each year, the largest months are far larger than a typical month.

**Step 4. Count the pay dates of the largest months.** Payroll is the largest debit to account 1090, and a count of the distinct posting dates of the payroll summaries shows how many payrolls each month received.

a. Copy the query of Step 3, with its comment, and paste the copy at the end of the script.
b. Edit the copy until it reads as below: change the comment, add PayDates to the outer SELECT list, and add the COUNT(DISTINCT ...) expression that calculates it to the inner one. Run it.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.2: the three largest months with their pay dates
   SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod, Gap, PayDates, GapRank
   FROM (
       SELECT FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod,
           ROUND(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit), 2) AS Gap,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN SourceDocumentType = 'PayrollSummary'
               THEN PostingDate END) AS PayDates,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY FiscalYear
               ORDER BY SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit) DESC) AS GapRank
       FROM GLEntry
       WHERE AccountID = 92 AND FiscalYear BETWEEN 2024 AND 2026
           AND SourceDocumentType <> 'WorkOrderClose'
       GROUP BY FiscalYear, FiscalPeriod
   ) AS monthly
   WHERE GapRank <= 3
   ORDER BY FiscalYear, GapRank;
   ```

c. Compare the PayDates of the months ranked first with those of the others.

The result, shown in @fig-11-06, points to the cause of the largest months. Charles River pays every two weeks, so most months have two pay dates, but a few have three, and the largest month of every year is one of them. The ledger records payroll when it is paid, and no entry at a month's end records the wages that were earned but not yet paid, so a month with three pay dates carries three payrolls.

![The Largest Months of the Gap and Their Pay Dates.](/visuals/svg/fig-11-06-gap-pay-dates.svg){#fig-11-06 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor and its result. The editor, on the tab Chapter11.sql, is scrolled to a query that ranks the months of each year by their gap in account 1090 in a derived table, counts the distinct pay dates of each month's payroll postings with COUNT DISTINCT over a CASE expression, and keeps the three largest months of each year. The grid shows nine rows, three for each of 2024, 2025, and 2026. The PayDates cells that show three pay dates are outlined, and they include the month ranked first in every year."}

**Step 5. Count the pay dates of every month.** Conditional aggregation, from Tutorial 11.1, puts the pay dates of each year in a column of its own, so that every month can be compared with the same month of the other years.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.2: pay dates by month, one column per year
   SELECT FiscalPeriod,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN FiscalYear = 2024
           THEN PostingDate END) AS Pay2024,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN FiscalYear = 2025
           THEN PostingDate END) AS Pay2025,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN FiscalYear = 2026
           THEN PostingDate END) AS Pay2026
   FROM GLEntry
   WHERE AccountID = 92 AND FiscalYear BETWEEN 2024 AND 2026
       AND SourceDocumentType = 'PayrollSummary'
   GROUP BY FiscalPeriod
   ORDER BY FiscalPeriod;
   ```

b. Find the months with three pay dates in each year.
c. Add up the pay dates of each year.

Each year has two months with three pay dates. July 2026 had three and July 2025 two, while August 2025 had three and August 2026 two, which explains the two comparisons of Step 2 that stood out. The months with three pay dates are not months of worse performance. Single months of this account are unreliable, but a year-to-date or trailing total is not, because over a year the pay dates even out. They do not quite even out between years. January 2024 shows no pay date at all, because the data begins in January and the manufacturing part of the year's first payroll was posted to the variance account instead, so fiscal 2024 charged two payrolls fewer than the later years. Part of the growth from fiscal 2024 comes from the calendar.

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Under accrual accounting, wages that employees have earned but not yet been paid at the end of a period are an expense of that period and a liability at its end. A company that closes its books every month usually records them with an accrual entry at the month's end, reversed when the payroll is paid. The Charles River ledger has no such entry for its wages, so its monthly payroll cost follows the pay calendar. An analyst who meets a lumpy monthly series should ask how its postings are timed before reading anything into a single month.
:::

**Step 6. Rank the work centers by the hours recorded against their plan.** Each work order operation records its planned hours and its work center, and the direct labor time is recorded against the operation. Only the operations that ended by the last day with time records are counted, so that no operation is compared with time that has not yet been recorded.

a. Type and run the query below.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.2: work centers ranked by hours recorded against plan
   SELECT EndYear, WorkCenterName,
       RecordedHours - PlannedHours AS ExcessHours,
       ROUND(RecordedHours / PlannedHours, 2) AS RecordedPerPlanned,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY EndYear
           ORDER BY RecordedHours / PlannedHours DESC) AS CenterRank
   FROM (
       SELECT strftime('%Y', op.ActualEndDate) AS EndYear,
           wc.WorkCenterName,
           ROUND(SUM(op.PlannedLoadHours), 0) AS PlannedHours,
           ROUND(SUM(lab.Hours), 0) AS RecordedHours
       FROM WorkOrderOperation AS op
           INNER JOIN WorkCenter AS wc ON wc.WorkCenterID = op.WorkCenterID
           LEFT JOIN (
               SELECT WorkOrderOperationID,
                   SUM(RegularHours + OvertimeHours) AS Hours
               FROM LaborTimeEntry
               WHERE LaborType = 'Direct Manufacturing'
               GROUP BY WorkOrderOperationID
           ) AS lab ON lab.WorkOrderOperationID = op.WorkOrderOperationID
       WHERE op.ActualEndDate <= (SELECT MAX(WorkDate) FROM LaborTimeEntry)
       GROUP BY EndYear, wc.WorkCenterName
   ) AS centers
   ORDER BY EndYear, CenterRank;
   ```

b. Compare the RecordedPerPlanned column across the work centers and years.

The result ranks the five work centers within each year. The condition on ActualEndDate also leaves out the operations that have not ended, because a comparison with NULL is never true. The pattern is lopsided. Packing and Quality Assurance record far more direct hours than their operations planned, several times more by fiscal 2026, while Assembly, Cutting, and Finishing record well under their plans. Quality Assurance plans so few hours that its ratio is high on a small base, and Packing holds nearly all the excess hours.

**Step 7. Add the plant's total.** A window with PARTITION BY but no ORDER BY covers its whole partition, so it can put each year's total beside every work center.

a. Copy the query of Step 6, with its comment, and paste the copy at the end of the script.
b. Edit the copy until it reads as below: change the comment, type a comma after `AS CenterRank`, and add the PlantExcessHours column below it. Run it.

   ```sql
   -- Tutorial 11.2: the ranking with the plant's excess hours
   SELECT EndYear, WorkCenterName,
       RecordedHours - PlannedHours AS ExcessHours,
       ROUND(RecordedHours / PlannedHours, 2) AS RecordedPerPlanned,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY EndYear
           ORDER BY RecordedHours / PlannedHours DESC) AS CenterRank,
       SUM(RecordedHours - PlannedHours) OVER (PARTITION BY EndYear)
           AS PlantExcessHours
   FROM (
       SELECT strftime('%Y', op.ActualEndDate) AS EndYear,
           wc.WorkCenterName,
           ROUND(SUM(op.PlannedLoadHours), 0) AS PlannedHours,
           ROUND(SUM(lab.Hours), 0) AS RecordedHours
       FROM WorkOrderOperation AS op
           INNER JOIN WorkCenter AS wc ON wc.WorkCenterID = op.WorkCenterID
           LEFT JOIN (
               SELECT WorkOrderOperationID,
                   SUM(RegularHours + OvertimeHours) AS Hours
               FROM LaborTimeEntry
               WHERE LaborType = 'Direct Manufacturing'
               GROUP BY WorkOrderOperationID
           ) AS lab ON lab.WorkOrderOperationID = op.WorkOrderOperationID
       WHERE op.ActualEndDate <= (SELECT MAX(WorkDate) FROM LaborTimeEntry)
       GROUP BY EndYear, wc.WorkCenterName
   ) AS centers
   ORDER BY EndYear, CenterRank;
   ```

c. Read the PlantExcessHours column of each year.

The result, shown in @fig-11-07, adds one column to the ranking of Step 6. The window `OVER (PARTITION BY EndYear)` adds up the excess hours of all five work centers in each year, and the total is negative in every year: the plant as a whole recorded fewer direct hours than its operations planned. If Packing were simply slow, Assembly would not be recording less than its plan at the same time. Hours that move from the start of the routing, the sequence of operations each work order follows, to its end while the total stays within plan point instead to time recorded against the wrong operations. That is a finding to investigate, not yet an explanation.

![Work Centers Ranked by Hours Recorded Against Plan.](/visuals/svg/fig-11-07-work-center-rank.svg){#fig-11-07 fig-alt="A mock of the Execute SQL editor and its result. The editor, on the tab Chapter11.sql, shows the start of a query that compares the direct labor hours recorded against each work center's operations with their planned load hours, by the year in which the operations ended, in a derived table. The outer query calculates the excess hours and the ratio of recorded to planned hours, ranks the work centers with RANK over a window partitioned by year, and totals the excess hours of each year with SUM over the same partition. The grid is scrolled to the five work centers of 2026. Packing and Quality Assurance rank first and second with about four times their planned hours, and those rows are outlined, while the plant's total excess is negative."}

**Checkpoint.** Check that:

- the year-to-date gap restarts each January, and its December figure grew in each year;
- the same-month comparison is NULL for fiscal 2024 and shows larger gaps in most months of fiscal 2026, with July and August 2026 far from the rest;
- the ranking query returns the three largest months of each year, filtered in the outer query;
- the largest month of each year has three pay dates, each year has two such months, and fiscal 2024 has two pay dates fewer than the later years;
- Packing and Quality Assurance record several times their planned hours, while the plant as a whole records fewer direct hours than planned;
- Chapter11.sql holds this tutorial's queries under their comments.

The window functions show that the gap grew from year to year and that its largest months come from the pay calendar, not from a few bad months. They also expose a pattern in the time records that the controller cannot explain from the numbers alone.
